blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an integer array `nums`, return **all the unique triplets** `[a, b, c]` taken from three different positions such that `a + b + c = 0`. The answer must not contain the same triplet twice, and the order of the triplets doesn't matter.

blocks.alt: The array [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]. Two triplets sum to zero: [-1, -1, 2] and [-1, 0, 1]. Using the other -1 in [-1, 0, 1] would give the same triplet again, so it only counts once.

elements.text: two different -1s, but [-1, 0, 1] is listed only once
elements.originalText: two different -1s, but [-1, 0, 1] is listed only once

blocks.text: There are two separate challenges here: finding triplets that sum to 0 **fast**, and making sure each triplet appears **once**, even when the array has repeated values.
Three nested loops try every combination of three positions. To drop duplicates, sort each triplet that works and keep it in a set.
**Time O(n³), space O(m)** for the m triplets in the set. With 3,000 numbers (LeetCode's limit) that's about 4.5 billion triplets — far too slow.
2. Optimal: fix one number, then Two Sum with a hash set

Once `nums[i]` is fixed, we need two later numbers that add up to `-nums[i]` — that's **Two Sum**. As `j` walks forward, a hash set of the values between `i` and `j` tells us in O(1) whether the third number, `-nums[i] - nums[j]`, has already appeared.
**Time O(n²), space O(n + m).** One whole loop is gone. But we still lean on hashing twice — a set per `i` to find the third number, and another set to throw away duplicate triplets.
3. Best solution: sort, then squeeze with two pointers
**Sort the array first.** Two good things happen at once:

items: For a fixed `nums[i]`, the pair can be found with **two pointers** instead of a hash set: `left` starts just after `i`, `right` at the end. Sum too small? Only a bigger left value helps: `left++`. Too big? `right--`.

**Equal values sit side by side**, so duplicates are easy to skip: if `nums[i]` equals the value before it, every triplet it could start has already been found. After recording a triplet, also step `left` past copies of the same value.

blocks.alt: The sorted array [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]. i points at the first -1, left at the second -1, right at 2. The sum is -1 + -1 + 2 = 0, a triplet. The rules: sum below 0 moves left forward, sum above 0 moves right back, a sum of 0 is recorded and both pointers move inward.
blocks.caption: Sorting turns "find a pair" into a squeeze from both ends, and lines up duplicates so they can be skipped.

blocks.text: **Time O(n²), space O(1)** extra, apart from the sort and the output. Sorting costs O(n log n), and each fixed `i` squeezes the rest of the array once. A small extra speed-up: once `nums[i] > 0`, every later number is positive too, so you can `break`.

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n³) time, O(m) space. Optimal: O(n²) time, O(n + m) space. Best: O(n²) time, O(1) space.

blocks.text: Here **m** is the number of triplets found. The optimal and best solutions share O(n²) time — the best one wins by dropping both hash sets, which makes it faster in practice and lighter on memory.

items: **Fewer than three numbers** — return `[]`; the loop never starts.

blocks.text: The same "fix one, squeeze the rest" structure solves **3Sum Closest** and **4Sum** (fix two, squeeze the rest: O(n³)).
